fullName: Coherent Surface Scattering Imaging beamline: station 9-ID-D and the 9-ID-GT 'Grand Tube'

status2026.detail: Operations of the old 9-ID (USAXS, Bionanoprobe) were suspended on 1 August 2022 and the old enclosures were removed by 22 December 2022 (9-ID home page; 9-ID news). The Grand Tube was unloaded in four sections in August 2023 and installed in September–October 2023 (APS-U pictures 2023; APS-U update Sep 2023; 9-ID news). The user manual says 'Since first light in 2024-2, 9-ID operates with a single revolver undulator' (9-ID source slide); that date must refer to the source and front end, because X-rays could not enter 9-ID-A before its shielding verification on 18 December 2024. 9-ID-A and 9-ID-MH were verified on 18 December 2024, 9-ID-D and the Grand Tube (9-ID-GT) on 28–30 January 2025 (9-ID news; 9-ID home page). Technical commissioning began on 3 February 2025; 9-ID 'transitioned to full operations' on 14 March 2026. Run 2026-2 (from 27 May 2026) gave 50% of beamtime through the Beamtime Allocation Committee, and run 2026-3 (from 9 September 2026) gives 80% to General User Proposals for GI-SAXS/WAXS/XPCS and CSSI (9-ID home page). The Beamline Directory lists 9-ID-D as 'Operational/Accepting General Users', with on-site access. Still incomplete compared with the 2019 design: only the downstream undulator slot is filled (9-ID source slide; APS ID table 2026), and no liquid-surface diffractometer or multilayer monochromator appears in the as-built component lists (9-ID user manual).

tagline: X-rays skim across chips and thin films like skipping stones; a 20-metre vacuum tube catches the faint speckle that reveals their nanoscale structure.
summary: Many technologies live in layers thinner than a soap bubble, such as chips and solar-cell films, on thick supports that get in the way of a beam shone straight through. The Coherent Surface Scattering Imaging (CSSI) beamline instead skims a coherent X-ray beam, one whose waves march in step, across the surface at a fraction of a degree, like a stone skipping on a pond. Every bump and buried edge scatters a little of it into a grainy interference pattern called speckle. A computer works backwards from the speckle to a 3D image, and the way the speckle flickers shows films flowing or reorganising over times from a thousandth of a second to many minutes. Each speckle grain must span several pixels to be read, so the cameras ride up to 22 m from the sample inside the Grand Tube, a 20-metre walk-in vacuum vessel. The beamline entered full operation in March 2026.

whatAPSUEnables.text: Speckle imaging works only with coherent X-rays, the part of the beam whose waves march in step. Before the upgrade about 0.05% of the APS beam at 10 keV was coherent, and in a 2012 test, recording one usable speckle pattern from an oversized gold test object took a few hours. The upgraded ring narrows the electron beam horizontally from about 275 µm to 12–15 µm (root-mean-square width), depending on mode, so a few percent of the light is now coherent, enough to measure realistic samples quickly and follow them as they change. When photon counts set the limit, speckle movies gain even more: at equal picture quality, acquisition time, contrast and pixel count, doubling the coherent flux cuts the shortest measurable time fourfold, so a hundredfold gain brings changes about 10,000 times faster within reach in principle, though the camera's millisecond frame time sets the practical limit. Source estimates give roughly 100–200 times more coherent flux; the 2017 design promised 100–1,000 times, but it assumed a longer source than the single 2.35 m undulator now installed.
quantitative: Coherent fraction at 10 keV: ~0.05% before the upgrade (σx 275 µm, σy 10 µm) vs ~2.6% (round-beam mode) or ~6% (flat-beam mode) for the 2.35 m revolver on APS-U. Derived here from the 2024 storage-ring source parameters, using λ/4π per plane.

Horizontal coherence length 30 m from the source at 10 keV: ~2 µm before the upgrade vs ~48 µm (round) or ~41 µm (flat) on APS-U; vertical ~58 µm vs ~70–160 µm. Derived with ξ = λz/(2πΣ) from the 2024 storage-ring parameters.

Peak brilliance of the U21/U25 revolver: >10²² ph/s/mm²/mrad²/0.1%BW at 10 keV, 'two orders of magnitude higher than the current Undulator A' (PDR 2017; also the 9-ID source-characteristics slide). The 9-ID slide shows the U21 first harmonic at ~2 × 10²² near 10–11 keV vs ~1.1 × 10²⁰ peak for the old APS U33.
Before the upgrade the APS delivered 0.01–0.1% coherent photons across the hard X-ray range (PDR 2017).

The 2012 CSSI demonstration at 8-ID-E had ~10⁹ coherent ph/s at 7.35 keV with the detector 0.7 m from the sample; each pattern took a few hours and peaked at 3,000 counts. Resolution was 2.6 µm × 22 nm × 2.7 nm (along the beam × in-plane × surface-normal) (PDR 2017; Sun et al. 2012).

Design flux at 9-ID at 8.8 keV: 9.2 × 10¹³ ph/s/0.1%BW into 0.75 × 0.42 µm with the KB mirrors (3 × 2 coherent modes); 9.4 × 10¹³ into 3.5 × 1.7 µm with CRL-2; 3.4 × 10¹⁴ into 29 × 16 µm with the CRL-1 full beam (FDR 2019, Table 4.58). The Beamline Directory quotes ~1.2 × 10¹³ ph/s for the KB mode.

XPCS: at fixed signal-to-noise ratio the shortest accessible time scales as 1/brilliance², so a ~100× brilliance gain gives ~10⁴× shorter times (the 9-ID source slide's 'scales as (Brilliance)²' refers to this improvement factor). GI-XPCS at 9-ID targets 10⁻³ to 10³ s (Beamline Directory; Strzalka 2025).
Sample-to-detector distance: 2.9–21.8 m in vacuum (APS CSSI page) vs 0.7 m in the 2012 demonstration (PDR 2017).
The 9-ID source slide shows a coherent fraction of ~6% at 10 keV and ~2% at 25 keV for APS-U (U25/U21) vs ~5 × 10⁻⁴ and ~1.4 × 10⁻⁴ for the old APS (U33), a gain of ~100–150× (read from the plot).

The PDR (2017) promised 'two to three orders of magnitude increase in coherent flux' assuming 4.8 m of undulator. As built there is one 2.35 m device, so ~100–200× is the realistic gain (PDR 2017; 9-ID source slide; APS ID table 2026).

techniques.name: Coherent Surface Scattering Imaging
techniques.text: Coherent surface scattering imaging (CSSI) makes 3D pictures of tiny structures on a surface without a lens. A coherent beam grazes the sample at roughly 0.1–1°, near the critical angle below which the surface reflects X-rays almost completely, and the structures scatter part of it into speckle. The camera records only brightness, not the timing (phase) of the waves, so it sits far enough away that each speckle spans at least two pixels; this oversampling lets a computer recover the phases and rebuild the object (phase retrieval), using models that include reflections from the substrate. The 2012 proof of principle resolved 22 nm across the surface and 2.7 nm in height but only 2.6 µm along the beam, a gap that turning the sample a few degrees fills; later work pushed in-plane resolution below 5 nm.

techniques.name: Grazing-Incidence X-ray Photon Correlation Spectroscopy
techniques.text: Grazing-incidence X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (GI-XPCS) watches the speckle twinkle instead of freezing it. As structures on or just below the surface move, the speckle changes. Each region of the pattern corresponds to one length scale, and software measures how quickly that region stops resembling its earlier self, a decay traced by the correlation function g₂. How the decay rate varies with length scale tells motions apart: diffusion, ripples (capillary waves) that die away without oscillating on a thick, viscous film, or the steady, ballistic rearrangement of jammed material. Setting the beam just below or above the critical angle selects the top few nanometres or the whole film. At 9-ID the EIGER 16M camera, 3–20 m away in vacuum, covers times from a millisecond to 1,000 seconds.

techniques.name: Grazing-Incidence Small-Angle X-ray Scattering
techniques.text: Grazing-incidence small-angle X-ray scattering (GISAXS) measures the average size, spacing and shape of nanoscale features, such as pores, grains or stripes, across a whole film. The beam skims the film, and X-rays scattered to small angles encode structures from about a nanometre to a few hundred nanometres. Unlike CSSI it averages over everything the beam touches rather than imaging one object, and the analysis must account for reflections from the substrate (the distorted-wave Born approximation). Films can be annealed, exposed to solvent vapour, spin-coated or grown while they are measured, with the EIGER 16M in the Grand Tube providing long camera distances.

techniques.name: Grazing-Incidence Wide-Angle X-ray Scattering
techniques.text: Grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) records X-rays scattered to larger angles, which reveal how molecules or atoms are stacked in a thin film and which way its crystals point, the film's texture. That matters for materials such as solar-cell films and plastic electronics. At 9-ID a Pilatus 1M-F camera in air beside the diffractometer records up to 135 frames a second, so films can be followed while they are heated or cooled (about −180 to 300 °C on the Linkam stage), spin-coated or cycled electrochemically, with a robot arm to change samples.

techniques.name: Grazing-incidence multibeam X-ray holography (Lloyd's-mirror surface holography)
techniques.text: Grazing-incidence X-ray holography uses the flat substrate as a built-in mirror, as in Lloyd's 19th-century mirror experiment with visible light. X-rays that a nanoscale feature scatters straight toward the detector interfere with those it scatters down onto the substrate, which then reflect off it, and the resulting fringes form a hologram whose spacing encodes the feature's height above the surface. The effect is strongest just above the sample's horizon, at exit angles below about 0.3°, and away from the bright mirror reflection, so the fringes stand out on a dark background. Analysed with detailed scattering simulations, a single view can yield 3D shapes with nanometre or sub-nanometre precision, which suits processes that cannot be repeated.

scienceCases.title: Seeing buried nanocircuits in 3D without cutting the chip
scienceCases.text: Chip makers must check the exact width and height of tiny patterned lines, a task called critical-dimension metrology, but slicing a chip destroys it, and lens-free X-ray imaging that shines straight through the sample cannot handle patterns on a thick wafer without thinning it. CSSI and its holographic variant read the shape from X-rays reflected at grazing angles instead, leaving the wafer intact. The 2012 proof of principle reconstructed a gold 'Argonne' test pattern with 22 nm resolution across the surface and about 2.7 nm in height; later experiments at the APS and the PETRA III synchrotron reached better than 5 nm across the surface. The beamline's 2023 first-experiments workshop included a talk on semiconductor metrology from NIST, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology.

scienceCases.title: 3D shape from a single snapshot: an X-ray Lloyd's mirror
scienceCases.text: A 19th-century optics experiment, Lloyd's mirror, makes light interfere with its own reflection. At grazing angles a silicon substrate plays the mirror for X-rays, and the interference fringes form a hologram that encodes the height of surface features in a single image. In 2023, Chu and colleagues showed, with data from the PETRA III synchrotron and the pre-upgrade APS, that one grazing view of gold bars on silicon carries enough 3D information to recover the thicknesses of stacked bars with nanometre or sub-nanometre precision, modelling the scattering with a simulation of more than 5 million cells. At 9-ID this single-view mode is aimed at irreversible processes, followed as they happen.

scienceCases.title: Teaching computers to invert surface speckle (physics-informed reconstruction)
scienceCases.text: Standard lens-free imaging assumes each X-ray scatters only once, so the speckle is tied to the object by a simple Fourier transform, minus the phases that iterative algorithms recover. Near a mirror-like surface that fails, because X-rays also reflect between the substrate and the structure. New algorithms instead simulate the beam passing slice by slice through a 3D model (a multislice model) and adjust the model, with the automatic differentiation used to train neural networks, until simulated and measured speckle agree. A 2023 study, tested on a prototype measurement at 8-ID and on simulations assuming the upgraded source's 100-fold flux, reconstructed elongated 3D patterns from single frames; a 2026 framework set out how finely the speckle must be sampled and rebuilt isolated 3D objects from rotation series at only one or two incidence angles.

scienceCases.title: Plastic electronics that breathe while they work
scienceCases.text: Soft 'mixed conductors', polymers that carry both ions and electrons, are used in biosensors and swell and shrink as ions flow in and out. In a 2024 study, a film of the conducting polymer PEDOT:PSS was measured with grazing-incidence speckle movies (GI-XPCS) at the pre-upgrade 8-ID-I, at ten frames a second, while it was electrochemically switched on and off (doped and de-doped) in a liquid cell. The flickering speckle tracked internal strain and slow rearrangement: the structure does not simply return to where it started (hysteresis) and keeps evolving slowly when switched back on. At 9-ID such studies pair wide-angle scattering (GIWAXS), which shows the molecular packing, with GI-XPCS on the coherent beam, over a millisecond to 1,000 seconds.

scienceCases.title: Watching solar-cell films crystallise as they are spun
scienceCases.text: Perovskite solar-cell films crystallise as a liquid of their ingredients is spun on a disc and dries. Grazing-incidence wide-angle scattering (GIWAXS), recorded during 5-minute spin-coating runs of mixed 2D/3D halide perovskites (layered and bulk crystal forms), revealed two competing formation routes, called the 'solvate' and 'orientation' mechanisms, with the proportions of the ingredients deciding which wins, a lever for steering the film's structure. Those 2022 measurements were made on the grazing-incidence instrument of 8-ID-E, which has since moved to 9-ID. The 2019 design names the 3D structure of photovoltaic films as one of six priority research areas for CSSI, and 9-ID supports spin coating, thermal and solvent-vapour annealing, and users' own solar simulators.

scienceCases.title: How thin films flow, roughen and self-organise
scienceCases.text: A molten polymer film, even a very thin one, has a restless surface rippled by tiny capillary waves, and grazing-incidence speckle movies (GI-XPCS) time how fast they relax. Measurements on ultrathin molten polystyrene showed in 2007 that the standard capillary-wave model needs an elastic term, a shear modulus: the films behave partly like solids. Coherent small-angle scattering (GISAXS) also follows patterns as they self-organise, such as ripples carved by ion beams; a 2021 study at the NSLS-II synchrotron found that they relax most slowly at the length scales where their structure is strongest, an effect called de Gennes narrowing. Self-assembly at surfaces, capillary instabilities in confined geometries and the dynamics of interfaces are among the science drivers in the 2019 design.

scienceCases.title: At-wavelength metrology of coherence-preserving X-ray mirrors
scienceCases.text: Mirrors that preserve a coherent beam must match their ideal shape to a fraction of a nanometre: 9-ID's own focusing mirrors are specified to shape errors below 0.3 nm (horizontal) and 0.2 nm (vertical), as a root-mean-square average, to keep the focus no more than 3% larger than ideal. Testing such optics with the very X-rays they will reflect, called at-wavelength metrology, is one of CSSI's listed priority research areas. 9-ID-D also carries a compact X-ray wavefront sensor, designed by the APS optics group, just downstream of the CSSI sample station.

keyParameters.value: 6–25 keV, fully tunable
keyParameters.note: The 2019 design gave 6–30 keV (FDR 2019); the source slide says continuously tunable over 8–25 keV (9-ID source slide). The U25 array's first harmonic reaches down to ~4.6–5 keV, so the 6 keV floor is set by the optics and operations.

keyParameters.value: 0.6 × 0.35 µm to 3.5 × 1.7 µm (H × V) in coherent modes
keyParameters.note: 2019 design at 8.8 keV: KB mirrors 0.75 × 0.42 µm, CRL-2 3.5 × 1.7 µm, CRL-1 full beam 29 × 16 µm (FDR 2019).

keyParameters.label: Sample-to-detector distance (in vacuum)
keyParameters.note: The feature page gives 'working distance 2.9 to 21.8 m' without naming the reference sample, assumed here to be CSSI (APS CSSI page). Other figures: 3–20 m for GISAXS and GI-XPCS (Strzalka 2025), 'up to 23 m' in the design (MEDSI 2020) and '>20 m' (SPIE 2025).

keyParameters.label: Grand Tube (9-ID-GT)
keyParameters.value: ~20.5 m long, 2.75 m diameter stainless-steel vacuum vessel with an 8 mm wall, rated for pink beam
keyParameters.note: Sources differ: 20 m × 2.75 m (Struct. Dyn. 2025); '66-foot-long, ~nine feet in diameter' (APS CSSI page); '70-foot-long enclosure', 100,000 lb (APS News 2023); '20 m long, 3 m diameter' (APS-U news 2023); '20 meters long and three meters wide' (APS-U update, Sep 2023). The values 20.5 m, 2.75 m and 8 mm come from the 2020 shielding design study (Sunil 2020).

keyParameters.label: Detectors
keyParameters.value: In-vacuum EIGER 16M (400 fps, 550 fps burst); in-vacuum MM-PAD; in-air Pilatus 1M-F (135 fps)

insertionDevices.name: Revolver undulator APS21R25#5 – U21 array (APS21#10)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet revolver undulator (two magnet arrays on a rotating carriage)
insertionDevices.notes: 112 periods (length derived as 112 × 21 mm = 2.35 m; the slide says 2.3 m). Device minimum gap 8.5 mm, administrative minimum 8.72 mm, user minimum 9.0 mm; Keff 1.38 and E1 8.34 keV at 8.5 mm; total power 5.4 kW and power density 216 kW/mrad² at 200 mA. In the FDR design it supplies the high-flux 8.8 keV fundamental and its third harmonic (26.4 keV). Installed in the downstream slot, its centre ~1.25 m downstream of the straight-section centre (FDR). The 9-ID source slide calls it a 'Tandem revolver undulator – 2.3 m long (21 and 25 mm periods)' with 'continuous tunability over 8–25 keV'. ID table footnote: effective periods = N – 2 (APS ID table 2026). The estimated E1 at the 9.0 mm user minimum gap is ~8.9–9.0 keV, so the FDR's 8.8 keV U21 fundamental (K = 1.305) is just out of reach; the U25 array covers it.

insertionDevices.name: Revolver undulator APS21R25#5 – U25 array (APS25#8)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet revolver undulator (second array of the same device)
insertionDevices.notes: 94 periods; Keff 1.99 and E1 4.58 keV at 8.5 mm; total power 8.1 kW, power density 225 kW/mrad². Rotated into place instead of U21 to reach lower fundamentals; the first and third harmonics of the two arrays together cover 6–25 keV, or up to 30 keV (PDR 2017; 9-ID source slide).

insertionDevices.name: Upstream slot (planned planar U21, not installed)
insertionDevices.notes: FDR Table 3.13: '09-ID dual inline: upstream Planar 2.1, downstream Rev 2.5/2.1, phase shifter/corrector'; FDR Table 4.56 used both devices (4.6 m) for its flux estimates. As of September 2026 the upstream position is empty and 'capable of hosting a second undulator in the future' (9-ID source slide; APS ID table 2026).

source.canting: None. 9-ID is a dual-inline (non-canted) straight with a single device installed in the downstream slot; the beam leaves along the straight-section axis.
source.frontEnd: APS-U High Heat Load Front End (HHLFE; limits 21 kW total, 590 kW/mrad²): permanent-magnet clearing magnet, LPPS, storage-ring valve, burn-through fixed mask BTFM1, FM2, collimator, GRID XBPM1, FM3, photon shutter PS2 with intensity monitor IM1, safety shutters SS1/SS2, wall collimator through the ratchet wall, then on the exit table in 9-ID-A: exit mask (2 × 2 mm, with XBPM2) at 25.4 m and tungsten exit collimator (5 × 5 mm) at 26.1 m. 9-ID uses the windowless exit with a built-in differential pump (FDR ch. 3 Table 3.1, Sec. 3-2.1; FDR 2019 4-8.3). FDR design power through the 2 × 2 mm mask: 2.10 kW for U21 with two devices (K 1.305), 0.812 kW for U25 (K 1.939) (FDR 2019 Table 4.56).
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: Electron beam at an ID straight (SR parameters 2024, August 2024). These are zero-current values; intrabeam scattering at 200 mA enlarges them somewhat. Round-beam mode: σx = 12.3 µm, σy = 8.26 µm, σx′ = 2.34 µrad, σy′ = 3.47 µrad (28.7 pm in each plane). Flat-beam mode (κ = 0.1): 14.5 / 3.08 µm and 2.75 / 1.29 µrad. Single-electron photon terms for L = 2.35 m (derived, σr = √(2λL)/4π, σr′ = √(λ/2L)): 1.9 µm / 5.1 µrad at 10 keV and 1.2 µm / 3.2 µrad at 25 keV. The photon divergence dominates, so the photon source is ~12.5 × 8.5 µm rms and ~5.6 × 6.2 µrad rms at 10 keV (round mode). The PDR quoted APS-U ranges of σx 5–30 µm and σy 2–14 µm vs 275 / 10 µm before the upgrade (PDR 2017, Table 6.18).

branches.name: 9-ID single line (pink or monochromatic)
branches.description: One beam path, with no canting or branching. In monochromatic mode the HDCM displaces the beam horizontally: at 42.38 m the single-energy beam runs ~10 mm outboard of the pink-beam path (XBPM drawing), and masks in 9-ID-A and 9-ID-MH (the dual-aperture PM-5 and the pink beam stop BS-2) handle both paths. Three sample positions share the line inside 9-ID-D: the CSSI solid-sample station (54.992 m), the GI-XPCS hexapod (~55.9 m) and the GIXS diffractometer (56.590 m), all using the Grand Tube detectors downstream.

components.name: Empty upstream undulator slot
components.distanceNote: Approximate: the mirror image of the downstream device's position (+1.25 m, FDR Table 4.56); not given explicitly in any source. Drawn as an empty outline.
components.text: An empty parking space for a second undulator. The straight section of the electron ring has room for two magnet arrays in a row, and the 2019 design put a conventional flat (planar) undulator with a 21 mm period here, 4.6 m of undulator in all with its neighbour, to make the beam brighter still. As of September 2026 only the downstream slot is filled; the beamline manual says this one can host a second undulator in the future.

components.name: Revolver undulator U21/U25 (APS21R25#5)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.56: the revolver's centre is 1.25 m downstream of the centre of the straight section, the origin for all distances on this beamline.
components.text: The light source. An undulator is a row of strong magnets, alternating north and south, above and below the electron beam; it makes the electrons slalom so that the light from every bend adds up into a narrow, intense X-ray beam. This one is a 'revolver' with two magnet arrays on a rotating mount, one repeating every 21 mm and one every 25 mm: staff swing in whichever gives more light at the chosen energy, then tune it by changing the magnet gap. Using each array's fundamental energy and its third harmonic (three times higher), it covers 6–25 keV, with about 100 times the peak brightness of the old APS undulator near 10 keV. It is 2.35 m long and has been the straight's only undulator since 2024.

components.name: High-heat-load front end (windowless, in the tunnel)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: the front end occupies roughly 14–23 m inside the tunnel. 19.4 m is the documented position of the first beam-position monitor and upstream mask in APS-U front ends (FDR Table 3.9); element positions for 9-ID's front end are not published.
components.text: The gatekeeper between the accelerator and the beamline, inside the concrete shielding of the ring tunnel. Water-cooled masks absorb the outer part of the beam, monitors check where it points, and safety shutters can stop it in an instant; this standard high-heat-load design of the upgraded APS is rated for 21 kW. It has no exit window: a differentially pumped section, which removes gas in stages, keeps the vacuums apart instead, because even a thin window would blemish the orderly beam that CSSI depends on.

specs.main elements: clearing magnet, masks, GRID-XBPM, photon and safety shutters

components.name: Ratchet shield wall (with wall collimator)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: ~22.1–23.6 m by analogy with the 28-ID ray-trace plan used in the CHEX dossier; not documented for 9-ID.
components.text: The thick concrete wall between the accelerator tunnel and the experiment hall. The X-rays leave the tunnel through a small opening lined with a metal collimator, so radiation cannot stream out alongside the beam. Its position, about 22–24 m from the source, is estimated from other APS sectors.

components.name: Front-end exit mask (2 × 2 mm, with XBPM2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.57.
components.text: A water-cooled metal block with a 2 mm square hole, the last part of the front end. It passes only the bright central part of the beam into the beamline and soaks up the rest as heat. A second X-ray beam-position monitor (XBPM2) is built into it, and behind it a differential pump, not a beryllium window, separates the vacuums.

components.name: Front-end exit collimator (tungsten, 5 × 5 mm)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.57.
components.text: A tungsten block with a 5 mm square hole. It stops bremsstrahlung, very-high-energy radiation made when ring electrons collide with leftover gas atoms, from travelling down the beamline alongside the X-rays.

components.name: Slits SL-1 (white beam, 9ID-SL-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.57 (high-heat-load white-beam slits with tungsten edge inserts); labelled 'Slits, PB 9ID-SL-1' as built.
components.text: Four movable jaws with tungsten edges that trim the raw beam to about a millimetre square, so the first mirror receives only the part it can use. They are built for heavy heat loads, because here the beam is still 'white', carrying every energy the undulator makes.

components.name: Mirror MR-1 (flat, horizontal deflection; 9ID-MR-1)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): scaled from the as-built 9-ID-A layout drawing (9-ID user manual, ELOG 897) between two points fixed in the 2019 design, slits SL-1 at 27.1 m and the enclosure's downstream wall at ~36.9 m. The 2019 design put the mirror at 28.25 m.
components.text: The first optic: a flat, water-cooled, ultra-smooth mirror set at a glancing angle of a few thousandths of a radian, a small fraction of a degree. At such angles X-rays reflect only below a cutoff energy, so the mirror passes the useful X-rays on and leaves the highest energies behind; in the 2019 design it absorbed about two-thirds of the 474 W reaching it. Coating stripes of platinum, silicon and chromium, chosen by moving the mirror, set the cutoff together with the angle. Like every beam-steering optic before the final focusing mirrors, it deflects the beam sideways rather than up, a common choice at beamlines that need a steady, coherent beam.

components.name: Secondary collimator SC-1 (9ID-SC-1)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): scaled from the as-built 9-ID-A layout drawing (9-ID user manual, ELOG 897) between two points fixed in the 2019 design, slits SL-1 at 27.1 m and the enclosure's downstream wall at ~36.9 m. The 2019 design had it at 29.1 m.
components.text: A heavy-metal block with a small opening, just after the first mirror. It catches radiation scattered off the mirror, along with stray high-energy radiation from the ring, so neither can travel on down the beamline.

components.name: Beam flag BD-1 (diamond screen; 9ID-BD-1)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): scaled from the as-built 9-ID-A layout drawing (9-ID user manual, ELOG 897) between two points fixed in the 2019 design, slits SL-1 at 27.1 m and the enclosure's downstream wall at ~36.9 m. The 2019 design had it at 29.5 m.
components.text: A diamond screen that can be lowered into the beam. It glows where the X-rays hit, and a camera watching it shows the beam's position and shape, at about 16 µm per pixel. With the first mirror moved out of the way, it shows the direct beam from the undulator.

components.name: White-beam stop PM-1 (9ID-PM-1)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): scaled from the as-built 9-ID-A layout drawing (9-ID user manual, ELOG 897) between two points fixed in the 2019 design, slits SL-1 at 27.1 m and the enclosure's downstream wall at ~36.9 m.
components.text: A cooled absorber for the raw 'white' beam, which still carries every energy. The first mirror deflects the useful beam slightly sideways, so anything that carries straight on, unreflected, lands here, and only the reflected beam continues.

components.name: Movable photon mask PM-2 ('DAMM'; 9ID-PM-2)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): scaled from the as-built 9-ID-A layout drawing (9-ID user manual, ELOG 897) between two points fixed in the 2019 design, slits SL-1 at 27.1 m and the enclosure's downstream wall at ~36.9 m.
components.text: A movable photon mask, labelled 'DAMM' on the as-built drawings (the name is not explained publicly), that can be positioned to block or pass selected parts of the beam and protect the equipment downstream. The radiation shielding of the beamline was designed on the assumption that the beam is defined by a pinhole-like opening and two mirrors.

specs.tag: 9ID-PM-2 on the layout drawing (the manual list's '9ID-PM-1' is an evident slip)

components.name: Secondary collimator SC-2 (9ID-SC-2)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): scaled from the as-built 9-ID-A layout drawing (9-ID user manual, ELOG 897) between two points fixed in the 2019 design, slits SL-1 at 27.1 m and the enclosure's downstream wall at ~36.9 m.
components.text: Another heavy-metal collimator, just ahead of the second mirror, that catches stray scattered radiation so it cannot travel on down the beamline.

components.name: Mirror MR-2 (bendable, horizontal deflection; 9ID-MR-2)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): scaled from the as-built 9-ID-A layout drawing (9-ID user manual, ELOG 897) between two points fixed in the 2019 design, slits SL-1 at 27.1 m and the enclosure's downstream wall at ~36.9 m. The mirror is not in the 2019 design.
components.text: A second glancing-angle mirror that bounces the beam back parallel to its original path, a little to one side. It can be gently bent to adjust how the beam converges and carries the same coating stripes as the first mirror. The extra reflection strips out more of the unwanted high-energy X-rays and blocks any straight line of sight back to the source, one reason the steel Grand Tube can serve as its own radiation shield: the shielding study assumed two mirrors at 3.0 mrad or more. The 2019 design had a single mirror, and the as-built angles are not published.

specs.coating stripes: same 4 stripes as MR-1 (logged on Cr)
specs.design basis: shielding study assumed two mirrors at ≥ 3.0 mrad

components.name: Photon mask PM-3 (9ID-PM-3)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): scaled from the as-built 9-ID-A layout drawing (9-ID user manual, ELOG 897) between two points fixed in the 2019 design, slits SL-1 at 27.1 m and the enclosure's downstream wall at ~36.9 m.
components.text: A cooled mask that absorbs stray beam after the second mirror, protecting the hardware downstream. It is rated for 'pink' beam, the mirror-filtered beam that still holds a band of energies before the monochromator picks one.

components.name: Beam flag BD-2 (9ID-BD-2)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): scaled from the as-built 9-ID-A layout drawing (9-ID user manual, ELOG 897) between two points fixed in the 2019 design, slits SL-1 at 27.1 m and the enclosure's downstream wall at ~36.9 m.
components.text: A second diamond screen and camera, lowered into the beam to check its position and shape after the two mirrors. It can show both the raw white beam and the mirror-filtered pink beam.

components.name: Photon mask PM-4 (9ID-PM-4)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): scaled from the as-built 9-ID-A layout drawing (9-ID user manual, ELOG 897) between two points fixed in the 2019 design, slits SL-1 at 27.1 m and the enclosure's downstream wall at ~36.9 m.
components.text: A protective mask that trims stray pink beam, the mirror-filtered beam of many energies, just before it enters the monochromator. Anything outside its opening ends up as heat in the block rather than on the crystals.

components.name: Bremsstrahlung collimator BC-1 (9ID-BC-1)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): scaled from the as-built 9-ID-A layout drawing (9-ID user manual, ELOG 897) between two points fixed in the 2019 design, slits SL-1 at 27.1 m and the enclosure's downstream wall at ~36.9 m. The manual lists it between PM-4 and SL-2; the 2019 design had it at 34.2 m.
components.text: A dense collimator that stops bremsstrahlung, very-high-energy radiation made when ring electrons hit leftover gas atoms, from following the beam. It is one link in the beamline's radiation-safety chain, placed just before the monochromator.

components.name: Slits SL-2 (pink beam, 9ID-SL-2)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): scaled from the as-built 9-ID-A layout drawing (9-ID user manual, ELOG 897) between two points fixed in the 2019 design, slits SL-1 at 27.1 m and the enclosure's downstream wall at ~36.9 m. The 2019 design had it at 29.9 m; it moved downstream when the second mirror was added.
components.text: Adjustable horizontal and vertical slits that trim the pink beam, the mirror-filtered beam of many energies, to the size the monochromator needs. The 2019 design placed them earlier; they moved downstream when the second mirror was added.

components.name: Monochromator HDCM (horizontal double-crystal, LN2-cooled; 9ID-MN-1)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): scaled from the as-built 9-ID-A layout drawing (9-ID user manual, ELOG 897) between two points fixed in the 2019 design, slits SL-1 at 27.1 m and the enclosure's downstream wall at ~36.9 m. The 2019 design had it at 30.65 m.
components.text: The monochromator: two perfect silicon crystals that pass a single X-ray energy out of the pink beam. Each crystal reflects only the wavelength that fits the spacing of its atomic layers at the angle it is turned to (Bragg diffraction); in the 2019 design, 8.8 keV needed 13.0°. The crystals are chilled with liquid nitrogen so the heat they absorb, about 160 W in that design, does not distort them, and a fixed-exit design keeps the outgoing beam in place as the energy changes. Like the mirrors, they deflect sideways rather than up, so the single-energy beam runs about 10 mm to the side of the pink beam's path.

specs.flag inside: diamond + CdWO₄ screen 'Flag3 9ID-BD-3' (tag also used for XBPM-1)

components.name: Dual-aperture mask PM-5 (9ID-PM-5)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): scaled from the as-built 9-ID-A layout drawing (9-ID user manual, ELOG 897) between two points fixed in the 2019 design, slits SL-1 at 27.1 m and the enclosure's downstream wall at ~36.9 m.
components.text: A mask with two openings: one on the pink beam's path and one on the single-energy beam's, which runs about 10 mm to the side after the monochromator. It lets either beam through while blocking everything else, so the line can run in either mode.

components.name: Shielded transport pipe (9-ID-A to 9-ID-MH)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: between the 9-ID-A wall (~36.9 m, FDR Fig. 4.51) and the mini-hutch (~41.5 m).
components.text: A shielded vacuum pipe on stands that carries the beam about 5 m across the open hall floor, from the first optics enclosure to the mini-hutch. Its shielding contains any scattered radiation along the way.

components.name: Pink-beam stop BS-2 (with gate valve GV-5; 9ID-BS-2)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): order from the as-built 9-ID-MH layout and component list (9-ID user manual, ELOG 898), anchored to the surveyed beam-position monitor 9ID-BD-3 at 42.38 m.
components.text: A beam stop at the entrance of the mini-hutch that blocks the pink beam, the mirror-filtered beam of many energies, whenever only the single-energy beam is wanted downstream. The single-energy beam passes about 10 mm to one side of it. Gate valve GV-5 alongside can seal off the vacuum sections.

components.name: Beam-position monitor XBPM-1 (Sydor; 9ID-BD-3)
components.distanceNote: Exact: 42.380 m on the XBPM drawing; a survey on 3 December 2024 gave 42.4186 m.
components.text: A beam-position monitor that continuously reports exactly where the beam is, so drifts can be spotted and corrected. It sits midway between the pink and single-energy beam paths, 10 mm apart here, and moves up to 13 mm sideways to measure either; a 22 mm opening lets the beam bypass it. Surveyed at 42.4 m from the source, it is one of the few points on the line with a published as-built position.

components.name: Slits SL-3 (pink beam, 9ID-SL-3)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): order from the as-built 9-ID-MH layout and component list (9-ID user manual, ELOG 898), anchored to the surveyed beam-position monitor 9ID-BD-3 at 42.38 m.
components.text: Slits that trim stray light from the edges of the beam before it reaches the first set of lenses. They are rated for the pink beam as well as the single-energy beam.

components.name: Photon shutter PH-1 (9ID-PH-1)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): order from the as-built 9-ID-MH layout and component list (9-ID user manual, ELOG 898), anchored to the surveyed beam-position monitor 9ID-BD-3 at 42.38 m.
components.text: A photon shutter that can block the X-ray beam inside the mini-hutch, ahead of the first lens set. Together with a second shutter at the hutch exit it lets the beam be stopped before the experiment station; its exact safety role is inferred from its name and position rather than documented.

components.name: Transfocator CRL-1 (9 lens cartridges; 9ID-RL-1)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): order from the as-built 9-ID-MH layout and component list (9-ID user manual, ELOG 898), anchored to the surveyed beam-position monitor 9ID-BD-3 at 42.38 m. The 2019 design put CRL-1 at 32.4 m, inside 9-ID-A.
components.text: The first stage of a zoom lens. It is a transfocator: nine cartridges of compound refractive lenses (CRLs), tiny curved lenses, presumably of beryllium, that slide in or out of the beam on command. X-rays bend only slightly in matter, so each lens focuses weakly; the cartridges hold 1 to 8 lenses with tip radii from 2 mm down to 0.1 mm, and the combination chosen sets the focal length. On its own it makes the larger spots used for grazing-incidence scattering and speckle-correlation measurements (XPCS), 29 × 16 µm in the 2019 design, and it prefocuses the beam for the lenses and mirrors downstream.

components.name: Beam flag BD-4 (9ID-BD-4)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): order from the as-built 9-ID-MH layout and component list (9-ID user manual, ELOG 898), anchored to the surveyed beam-position monitor 9ID-BD-3 at 42.38 m.
components.text: A screen and camera that check the beam after the first lens stage. It works with both the pink and the single-energy beam.

components.name: Shutter SH-1 (9ID-SH-1)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): order from the as-built 9-ID-MH layout and component list (9-ID user manual, ELOG 898), anchored to the surveyed beam-position monitor 9ID-BD-3 at 42.38 m. The 2019 design had a pink-beam shutter at 35.5 m.
components.text: The station shutter, at the exit of the mini-hutch. It can stop the beam before it enters the experiment station, 9-ID-D; the 2019 design listed it as a pink-beam shutter and placed it farther upstream.

components.name: Fast shutter (9ID-BI-8)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): order from the as-built 9-ID-D layout and component list (9-ID user manual, ELOG 895), anchored to the beam-position monitor 9ID-BD-5 at 53.43 m and the CSSI station at 54.992 m (ELOG 916). The 2019 design had slits at 47.7 m.
components.text: A quick shutter that opens only while a camera is recording, so delicate films receive no more X-rays than they need. Its timing is synchronised electronically with each detector exposure.

components.name: Attenuator AT-1 (filter foils; 9ID-AT-1)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: the 2019 design put filters at 48.2 m; as built they share the fast shutter's table (9-ID user manual).
components.text: A set of thin metal foils that can be dropped into the beam to dim it in steps when it is too strong for the sample or the camera. It works with both the pink and the single-energy beam.

components.name: Slits SL-4 (9ID-SL-4)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): order from the as-built 9-ID-D layout and component list (9-ID user manual, ELOG 895), anchored to the beam-position monitor 9ID-BD-5 at 53.43 m and the CSSI station at 54.992 m (ELOG 916).
components.text: Slits that clean up the beam's edges before the second lens set. Closed down further, they pass only a beam narrow enough for its waves to stay in step across it, the coherent part: the 2017 plan set such slits to about two coherence lengths (the width over which the waves stay in step) vertically and three horizontally.

components.name: Transfocator CRL-2 (10 lens cartridges; 9ID-RL-2)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: FDR Table 4.57 value; the as-built order is SL-4 → CRL-2 → SL-5 (9-ID user manual).
components.text: The second, stronger zoom-lens stage: ten cartridges of compound refractive lenses, holding 1 to 16 lenses each. It can focus the beam to a spot a few micrometres across, 3.5 × 1.7 µm at 8.8 keV in the 2019 design, while accepting only about six coherent 'modes', patches of the beam within which the waves are in step, so the speckle stays crisp.

components.name: Slits SL-5 (9ID-SL-5)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): order from the as-built 9-ID-D layout and component list (9-ID user manual, ELOG 895), anchored to the beam-position monitor 9ID-BD-5 at 53.43 m and the CSSI station at 54.992 m (ELOG 916).
components.text: The last slits before the focusing mirrors, trimming away stray light around the beam so that only the intended beam reaches them. Like the slits upstream, they are rated for the pink beam.

components.name: Beam-position monitor XBPM-2 (Sydor; 9ID-BD-5)
components.distanceNote: Exact: 53.432 m on the XBPM drawing; a survey on 3 December 2024 gave 53.3988 m.
components.text: A second beam-position monitor, just before the focusing mirrors, checking that the beam enters them exactly on target. Surveyed at 53.40 m, it sits at almost the same sideways offset as the first monitor 11 m upstream, which shows that the beam runs parallel to its original axis.

components.name: KB focusing mirrors (Kirkpatrick–Baez pair; 9ID-MR-3)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: the 2019 design put the vertical and horizontal KB mirrors 1.0 m and 0.8 m upstream of the 55 m sample (54.0 and 54.2 m); SPIE 2025 quotes a working distance of ~650 mm to the CSSI sample at 54.992 m.
components.text: The final focus: a Kirkpatrick–Baez (KB) pair of curved mirrors at right angles, the first squeezing the beam vertically and the second horizontally. Each is bent into a precise curve that brings the beam to a focus at the sample, about 650 mm past the last mirror, in a spot designed to be about half a micrometre across and limited only by diffraction, the unavoidable spreading of any wave. To keep that spot still the mirrors must hold their angle to 14–19 nanoradians, the angle a 1 cm coin subtends from 500–700 km away, and their surfaces may depart from the ideal shape by less than 0.3 nm. They sit in ultra-high vacuum on the same granite table as the CSSI sample station, watched by laser interferometers.

components.name: Window WN-1 (Be or SiN; 9ID-WN-1)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): order from the as-built 9-ID-D layout and component list (9-ID user manual, ELOG 895), anchored to the beam-position monitor 9ID-BD-5 at 53.43 m and the CSSI station at 54.992 m (ELOG 916).
components.text: A thin window of beryllium or silicon nitride, materials X-rays pass through easily. It separates the ultra-high vacuum around the focusing mirrors from the ordinary high vacuum of the sample chamber.

components.name: CSSI sample station (solid samples, in vacuum; 9ID-BI-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: 'CSSI-SSS: 54992' mm (9-ID user manual, ELOG 916).
components.text: The heart of CSSI: a vacuum chamber in which the sample stands on its edge, like a book on a shelf, while the focused beam grazes its surface at a fraction of a degree and the reflection fans out sideways into the Grand Tube. Flexure stages, which move by bending metal rather than sliding, position it to nanometres, checked by laser interferometers. At 1° a 1 µm height error slides the beam's footprint 57 µm along the surface, so the surface must be found to better than 50 nm, and the angle must hold to about 50 nanoradians. Rotation stages set the grazing angle and turn the sample a few degrees for 3D views, and the station shares a granite table with the focusing mirrors to cut relative motion.

components.name: Wavefront sensor (9ID-BD-6)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (±1 m): order from the as-built 9-ID-D layout and component list (9-ID user manual, ELOG 895), anchored to the beam-position monitor 9ID-BD-5 at 53.43 m and the CSSI station at 54.992 m (ELOG 916). It is listed directly after the CSSI station.
components.text: A compact sensor that measures the shape of the X-ray wave itself, its wavefront, to check that the mirrors and lenses deliver a clean, undistorted focus. Designed by the APS optics group, it sits just after the CSSI sample station; how it senses the wavefront is not described publicly.

components.name: GI-XPCS hexapod (Aerotech HEX500-350HL)
components.distanceNote: Approximate, derived: the hexapod stands 'downstream of CSSI Solid Sample Station on the stationary granite of the GIXS table' (9-ID instrument notes). The manual gives 1.552 m from the hexapod centre to KB-H and 1.818 m to KB-V; with KB-H ~0.65 m upstream of 54.992 m, that puts it near 55.9 m.
components.text: A six-legged robotic platform, a hexapod, that holds heavier sample cells rock-steady for GI-XPCS, which measures how surfaces move from the twinkling of their speckle. Changing the lengths of its six legs tilts and shifts its 500 mm platform in any direction. It is the same high-load Aerotech model as the rheometer hexapod at 8-ID-I, and arrived in October 2024.

components.name: GIXS diffractometer (GISAXS/GIWAXS, from 8-ID-E)
components.distanceNote: Exact: 'GIXS: 56590' mm (9-ID user manual, ELOG 916).
components.text: The workhorse station for films lying flat, moved here from the old 8-ID-E station. Films can be heated or cooled, annealed in solvent vapour, spin-coated or deposited while the X-rays watch their structure form, and a small robot arm changes samples. Wide-angle patterns go to a camera beside it in air, small-angle patterns to the EIGER camera in the Grand Tube.

components.name: GIWAXS detector Pilatus 1M-F (on motion system 9ID-BI-7)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: in air just downstream of and beside the GIXS sample; the position varies on the WAXS detector motion system (9-ID user manual).
components.text: A camera close to the film that catches X-rays scattered to wide angles, revealing how molecules and crystals are packed and which way they line up. This Pilatus 1M-F, with 172 µm pixels, works in air on its own motion system and records up to 135 frames a second.

components.name: Grand Tube (in-vacuum flight path, 9-ID-GT)
components.distanceNote: Approximate start. Detector distances of 2.9–21.8 m from the CSSI sample (APS CSSI page) put the detector at ~57.9–76.8 m; with a tube ~20.5 m long (Sunil 2020) the vessel spans ~57.4–77.9 m. The 2019 design's flight path ran 58.0–76.0 m. The 3D model draws the vessel from 57.5 to 78.0 m.
components.text: The Grand Tube: a walk-in steel vacuum vessel about 20 m long and 2.75 m across. Speckle grains are tiny close to the sample and grow in proportion to distance, so the cameras must be many metres away for each grain to cover several pixels, and the path is pumped to vacuum because air would scatter X-rays and drown the faint signal. The cameras ride inside on a carriage 2.9–21.8 m from the CSSI sample and can also move up, down and sideways. The 8 mm stainless-steel wall is itself the radiation shield, making the tube a certified X-ray enclosure. It weighs about 45 tonnes and arrived in four sections in August 2023.

specs.length: ~20.5 m (20 m; 66 ft; 70 ft in other sources)

components.name: EIGER 16M detector (in vacuum, on the carriage)
components.distanceNote: Movable: ~57.9–76.8 m (2.9–21.8 m from the CSSI sample, APS CSSI page); 75.0 m corresponds to a ~20 m camera length. The 3D model draws the carriage 20 m from the CSSI sample, with the EIGER beside the MM-PAD (an illustrative arrangement).
components.text: An 18-megapixel camera that counts single X-ray photons, working inside the tube's vacuum. Its 75 µm pixels are small enough that, 20 m from the sample, one speckle from a 0.75 µm spot at 8.8 keV spans about 50 of them across. It records 400 frames a second (550 in bursts) and moves on the carriage: far back to make the speckles big, off to the side to catch the wider angles that carry finer detail. It serves surface imaging (CSSI), small-angle scattering (GISAXS) and speckle-correlation measurements (GI-XPCS).

specs.format: ~4150 × 4370 px, ~311 × 328 mm (PDR value for the first-generation EIGER X 16M; as-built variant not published)
specs.vacuum rule: powered off while pumping or venting between 1 bar and 0.01 mbar

components.name: MM-PAD detector (mixed-mode, in vacuum)
components.distanceNote: Movable inside the Grand Tube; the exact mounting is not published. The 3D model puts it on the same carriage, 0.45 m ahead of the EIGER 16M and centred on the mirror-reflection spot (an illustrative arrangement).
components.text: A camera that can record the blinding mirror-like reflection and the faintest speckles in the same picture. Near the critical angle the reflection can reach 10¹¹ counts per second in one pixel while useful speckle is 8–10 orders of magnitude fainter; this mixed-mode pixel array detector (MM-PAD), developed at Cornell, combines charge integration with counting in every pixel to span that range. So no beam stop is needed in front of it, and CSSI keeps the low-angle data near the reflection that its reconstructions need. The version installed at 9-ID is not published.

specs.format (PDR): 256 × 384 px (PDR also quotes 47 × 49 mm, inconsistent with 38.4 × 57.6 mm from 150 µm pixels)
specs.peak rate it must handle: up to 10¹¹ counts/s per pixel near the critical angle
specs.vacuum interlock: power cut above a gauge reading of 10⁻³ (since June 2026)

components.name: End-of-line beam stop
components.distanceNote: Approximate: 'Beam Stop, PB' at 78.0 m in FDR Table 4.57 (labelled 8ID-BS-1, evidently a typo); the as-built end stop is not documented publicly.
components.text: A final block at the far end of the Grand Tube that safely absorbs whatever beam reaches the end of the line. It is rated for the full pink beam; the as-built stop is not documented publicly.

enclosures.name: Storage-ring tunnel / front end
enclosures.role: source (revolver undulator, downstream slot) and HHL front end
enclosures.notes: Straight-section limits are approximate (~5.4 m straight); the ratchet wall is placed at ~22.1–23.6 m by analogy with other APS-U sectors.

enclosures.name: 9-ID-A
enclosures.notes: Boundaries read from the scale of FDR Fig. 4.51 (±0.3 m); wedge-shaped in plan. Contains the front-end exit table, SL-1, MR-1, MR-2, masks and collimators, flags, SL-2, the HDCM and the dual-aperture mask PM-5. Shielding verified on 18 December 2024.

enclosures.name: Shielded transport
enclosures.role: shielded beam transport on the hall floor (9-ID-A to 9-ID-MH)
enclosures.notes: Between the 9-ID-A wall (~36.9 m, FDR Fig. 4.51) and the mini-hutch (~41.5 m); support stands ~2 m apart in the FDR plan.

enclosures.name: 9-ID-MH

instruments.name: CSSI solid-sample instrument (KB + solid sample station 9ID-BI-2)
instruments.text: The instrument built for lens-free 3D imaging of surfaces: the Kirkpatrick–Baez (KB) focusing mirrors and the solid-sample station, aligned to the beam on granite air-bearing stages. A chip-like sample stands on edge in high vacuum about 650 mm past the mirrors, held by flexure stages in five groups, from coarse alignment to fine scanning, and watched by capacitive sensors and laser interferometers. The design goals are a 500 nm diffraction-limited spot, mirror angles steady to 14–19 nanoradians and a sample steady to about 50 nanoradians. Installed in 2024–2025, it records its speckle with the EIGER 16M and the MM-PAD in the Grand Tube.
sampleEnvironments: In-plane (yaw) rotation series for tomographic CSSI

instruments.name: GIXS instrument (GISAXS / GIWAXS), migrated from 8-ID-E
instruments.text: The workhorse station for thin films lying flat, moved here from the old 8-ID-E station. It measures grazing-incidence small- and wide-angle scattering (GISAXS and GIWAXS): a Pilatus 1M-F in air beside the sample records wide angles, which reveal molecular packing, and the EIGER 16M 3–20 m away in the Grand Tube records small angles, which reveal nanoscale structure. Films can be heated, cooled, annealed in solvent vapour, spin-coated or deposited while being measured, and a robot arm changes samples. Data flow through automated workflows to high-performance computers for analysis.
sampleEnvironments: Linkam HFSX350-GI thermal stage (−180 to 300 °C per directory; −196 to 350 °C per manual)

instruments.name: GI-XPCS setup (high-load hexapod + Grand Tube)
instruments.text: Measures how fast surfaces and buried interfaces move by recording thousands of speckle frames and computing how quickly the pattern changes. Samples sit on a high-load hexapod on the stationary granite, and the EIGER 16M records the speckle 3–20 m away in vacuum, covering times from a millisecond to 1,000 seconds. Graphics processors compute the correlations in automated workflows.
sampleEnvironments: User sample cells on the hexapod

instruments.name: Grand Tube detector system (9-ID-GT)
instruments.text: A 20-metre walk-in vacuum 'corridor' with a detector carriage inside. Moving a camera far from the sample spreads each speckle over many pixels (oversampling), which phase retrieval needs; moving it sideways or up reaches larger scattering angles and so finer detail, and several positions can be combined to cover more of the pattern. The 8 mm stainless-steel wall is rated as shielding for the pink beam, and interlocks tied to the tube's pressure switch off the cameras' power or high voltage when conditions are unsafe for them.

geometryNotes:
CSSI uses a single, non-canted insertion-device line: a dual-inline straight with only the downstream revolver installed, its source point ~1.25 m downstream of the straight-section centre. All distances here are measured from the straight-section centre, as in the FDR tables.

Everything sits on the main experiment-hall floor (no long-beamline building): the 9-ID-A first optics enclosure (~23.6–36.9 m, wedge-shaped in plan per FDR Fig. 4.51), shielded transport, the small 9-ID-MH mini-hutch (~41.5–45 m, an as-built addition), more shielded transport, the 9-ID-D station (~47–57.5 m) and the free-standing Grand Tube 9-ID-GT (~57.5–78 m). The tube is its own pink-beam-rated shielding: a light-grey cylinder 2.75 m in diameter, built from ~4 flanged sections with stiffener rings and a dished downstream head, resting on saddles on the floor outside any hutch (APS photo; APS CSSI page). The line ends close to the hall's outer wall (~90 m available).

Optics: all deflections upstream of the KB mirrors are horizontal. MR-1 (flat) and MR-2 (bender) form a horizontal offset pair ~2.9 m apart in the layout. The HDCM also deflects horizontally; the single-energy beam runs ~10 mm outboard of the pink path at 42.4 m, so PM-5 has two apertures and the XBPM a bypass. The surveyed XBPM bodies at 42.42 m and 53.40 m sit at almost the same horizontal offset from the white-beam axis (X = −8.79 and −8.64 mm), so the downstream beam runs parallel to the original axis, displaced sideways (XBPM drawing).

The KB pair (vertical mirror first) is the exception: the vertical mirror deflects the beam vertically (2.5 mrad grazing in the FDR, i.e. ~5 mrad upward or downward; the direction is not documented) and the horizontal mirror horizontally, focusing ~0.65 m downstream. The beam height is ~1.4 m above the floor throughout (FDR).

Inside 9-ID-D (as-built isometric, 9-ID user manual): upstream optical table (fast shutter, attenuator) → slits SL-4 → CRL-2 transfocator stand → slits SL-5 and the XBPM-2 table → KB ultra-high-vacuum chamber on granite → window → round multi-port CSSI sample chamber on granite → stationary granite with the hexapod → GIXS diffractometer on translating granite with the in-air Pilatus WAXS detector arm → Grand Tube entrance flange in the downstream wall.

There are two sample geometries. CSSI samples stand with their surface *vertical*, so incidence and specular reflection lie in the horizontal plane and the reflected beam and exit angles spread sideways in the tube. GIXS samples lie *horizontal* (classic GISAXS), with exit angles vertical. The detector carriage moves along z and in x and y within the 2.75 m bore.

Exact as-built z positions are public only for the CSSI station (54.992 m), GIXS (56.590 m) and the two XBPMs (42.38 m and 53.43 m); other positions are estimates (±1 m). The deflection sense (inboard or outboard) of MR-1 and MR-2 is not documented; only the direction of the mono–pink offset is.

3D model: true distances along the beam. The real lateral offsets of the mirror pair (~17 mm for two ~3 mrad reflections 2.9 m apart) and of the HDCM (~10 mm) are invisible at hall scale, so the beam is drawn on one axis; MR-1 and MR-2 are drawn as an outboard periscope (sense undocumented). The Grand Tube axis is drawn 0.2 m above beam height so the vessel clears its saddles (the axis height is unpublished).

CSSI is shown with a 0.5° incidence angle, true but invisible at room scale: the chip faces inboard (side undocumented), so the specular reflection leaves at 1° and lands ~0.35 m inboard of the direct beam 20 m downstream, where the MM-PAD waits; the EIGER 16M sits further inboard at larger exit angles. A floating magnifier above the sample chamber repeats the geometry with the chip enlarged ×8 and the angles exaggerated ×24.

interactiveIdeas.title: Skip a stone with X-rays: the critical angle
interactiveIdeas.concept: A slider tilts a silicon wafer from 0 to 1° in front of an X-ray beam. Below the critical angle the beam reflects almost totally and only a few-nm-deep evanescent wave enters; above it the beam dives in. Show reflectivity curve, penetration depth and the footprint stretching across the wafer.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why surface X-ray methods work at tiny angles, how depth sensitivity is tuned, and why a 1 µm beam paints a ~0.2 mm stripe on the sample.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: αc = sqrt(2 δ), δ proportional to λ² ρe: Si αc ~0.20° (3.5 mrad) and Au ~0.50° at 8.8 keV, scaling as 1/E. Penetration depth below αc ~ λ/(4π sqrt(αc² – α²)) ~ a few nm (include β for absorption). Footprint = beam size / sin(α): 0.75 µm at 0.2° → ~215 µm. Yoneda peak at αf = αc.

interactiveIdeas.title: Speckle zoom: why the Grand Tube is 20 m long
interactiveIdeas.concept: Drag the EIGER/MM-PAD along the tube (2.9-21.8 m) and sideways; choose energy (6-25 keV) and focal spot (0.6-3.5 µm). The speckle pattern rescales live over a pixel grid; meters show oversampling ratio and the finest resolvable feature.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: The core trade-off of coherent imaging: far away = speckles big enough to sample (oversampling), close or off-axis = higher q = finer detail; the tube allows both by moving the detector in 3D.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Speckle size s ~ λ D / d (d = illuminated size projected normal to the exit direction); oversampling O = s/p ≥ 2 per dimension (Nyquist), ~5 preferred. Examples: 8.8 keV, D = 20 m, d = 0.75 µm → s ~3.8 mm (~50 EIGER pixels); 25 keV, d = 3.5 µm, D = 20 m → s ~0.28 mm (O ~1.9 with 150 µm MM-PAD pixels). Half-period resolution ~ π/q_max, q_max = (4π/λ) sin(theta_max): detector half-width 0.155 m at 20 m and 8.8 keV gives ~9 nm; at 2.9 m ~1.3 nm. In grazing incidence resolution is anisotropic (poor along the beam footprint) – rotation series fix this.

interactiveIdeas.title: Lloyd's mirror in the hard X-ray world
interactiveIdeas.concept: A glowing point (a nanoscale feature) floats above a mirror-like substrate. Move it up and down and watch interference fringes appear on a virtual detector near the horizon, then reverse: given fringes, guess the height.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How a substrate acts as a built-in reference beam, turning surface scattering into a hologram that encodes height from a single image.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Two paths: direct scattering and scattering reflected by the substrate (phase flip ~π near αf = 0 where Fresnel reflectance → 1). Fringe period in qz ~ 2π/(2d) for height d; strongest for αf < ~0.3° and αi above αc (Chu et al. 2023). Keep Fresnel reflectivity and absorption; it is dark-field (away from specular).

interactiveIdeas.title: Then and now: how orderly is the X-ray beam?
interactiveIdeas.concept: Two virtual pinholes (Young's double slit) at 30 m from the source: toggle between the 1996-2023 APS and APS-U sources and energies. Fringe visibility and the number of 'coherent modes' across the beam change dramatically, especially horizontally.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: What 'coherence' means and why the multi-bend-achromat upgrade made CSSI practical.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Transverse coherence length (rms) ξ = λ z/(2π Σ), Σ = sqrt(σe² + σr²), σr = sqrt(2 λ L)/(4π). At 10 keV, 30 m: APS-U xi_x ~48 µm (round mode), old APS ~2 µm; vertical ~70 µm vs ~58 µm. Coherent fraction per plane = (λ/4π)/(Σ Σ'): ~2.6% (round) / ~6% (flat) total at 10 keV vs ~0.05% before. Use SR parameters 2024 parameters; do not use the 2019 FDR 'brightness mode' as current. SR parameters 2024 values are zero-current; the 9-ID source slide (9-ID source slide) plots ~6% coherent fraction at 10 keV (~2% at 25 keV) for APS-U vs ~0.05% for the old APS, consistent with the flat-beam case. Show coherent FLUX (brilliance × (λ/2)²), not total flux, as the quantity that rose ~100×.

interactiveIdeas.title: Twinkle, twinkle: build a g₂ curve
interactiveIdeas.concept: A live speckle movie from a thin polymer film; the user chooses temperature (viscosity) and film thickness. A cursor-picked speckle's intensity trace feeds a real-time correlation function g₂(τ).
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How XPCS turns flicker into a relaxation time and how different motions (diffusion, capillary waves) leave different q-dependences.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: g₂(q,τ) = 1 + β |f(q,τ)|², f = exp(-Γ τ) for simple relaxation; diffusion Γ = D q²; overdamped capillary waves on thick films Γ = γ q/(2 η) (thin films: Γ ~ γ h³ q⁴/(3 η)); β (speckle contrast) < 1 set by coherence and pixel/speckle ratio. Fastest time limited by detector (~2 ms at 400-550 fps) and by photons: SNR ~ β * I * sqrt(T τ N); at fixed SNR the shortest τ scales as 1/brilliance². 9-ID window 10⁻³-10³ s.

interactiveIdeas.title: Zoom lens of beryllium: the transfocators
interactiveIdeas.concept: Toggle the 9 + 10 lens cassettes of CRL-1 and CRL-2 (binary stacks of R = 2000..100 µm lenses) and the KB mirrors to zoom the spot from ~30 µm to ~0.5 µm at the sample; see flux and number of coherent modes accepted.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How X-ray lenses work (weakly), why many lenses are stacked, and the trade-off between spot size and coherent flux.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Thin-lens focal length f = R/(2 N δ) for paraboloid lenses (Be δ ~4.4 × 10⁻⁶ at 8.8 keV, so N=1, R=100 µm gives f ~11 m), combine stacks with 1/f = sum; imaging 1/p + 1/q = 1/f; spot ~ source size x magnification convolved with diffraction ~λ/(2 NA). Use as-built cassettes (CRL design review), not the FDR 12-stack lists.

funFacts: The Grand Tube weighs about 100,000 lb (~45 t). It was unloaded at Argonne in four crated sections in August 2023, assembled in three weeks and installed at 9-ID in September–October 2023.
The KB mirrors must hold their angle to 14–19 nanoradians, the angle a 1 cm coin subtends seen from about 500–700 km away (MEDSI 2020, SPIE 2025; comparison derived).

In CSSI the mirror-like reflection can be as bright as the incoming beam while useful speckles are 8–10 orders of magnitude fainter, up to 10¹¹ counts/s per pixel near the critical angle, so a special mixed-mode detector (MM-PAD) replaces the usual beam stop.
The Grand Tube is big enough to walk inside: about 2.75 m (9 ft) across and ~20 m long. Entering it requires a formal access procedure.
Its 8 mm stainless-steel wall doubles as radiation shielding, so the tube itself is a certified X-ray enclosure (9-ID-GT) rather than a pipe inside a hutch.

The first CSSI demonstration (2012, APS 8-ID-E) used a CCD camera only 0.7 m from the sample that detected just ~0.13% of the scattered photons. It needed a few hours to record one pattern, peaking at 3,000 counts, from a gold 'Argonne' test pattern 400 µm long, 5 µm wide and 40 nm thick.
At a 1° grazing angle, raising the sample by 1 µm slides the beam footprint ~57 µm along the surface; the stage must find the surface to better than 50 nm.
Before the upgrade the horizontal coherence length 30 m from the source was only ~2 µm at 10 keV; at the upgraded APS it is ~40–50 µm (derived from the 2024 storage-ring parameters).
9-ID used to host the USAXS instrument (now at 12-ID-E) and the Bionanoprobe (now at 2-ID-D); its GIXS instrument moved in from 8-ID-E.
The holographic analysis echoes Humphrey Lloyd's 19th-century mirror-interference experiment, redone with hard X-rays and a silicon wafer as the mirror.

openQuestions: As-built z positions are public only for the CSSI station (54.992 m), GIXS (56.590 m) and the XBPMs (42.38 and 53.43 m); the '09-ID Beamline Component Reference Table' and the optics schematic are on access-restricted Box. All other positions here are FDR values or ±1 m estimates from isometric drawings.
The boundaries of 9-ID-MH (~41.5–45 m) and of the 9-ID-D / Grand Tube interface (~57.5 m) are estimates, and hutch widths are not published (the FDR plan figure appears anisotropically scaled).

As-built mirror incidence angles are not published (FDR: a single M1 at 2.4 mrad; the shielding analysis assumed two mirrors at ≥ 3.0 mrad). The fourth mirror stripe is unidentified, and whether MR-1 deflects inboard or outboard is unknown.

HDCM: the crystal set (FDR Si(111) only; PDR Si(111) + Si(220); the directory's 'High resolution' mode with ΔE/E = 2.8 × 10⁻⁵ would fit Si(311)) and the fixed-exit offset (FDR '2 mm offset' vs the ~10 mm pink–mono separation at 42.4 m in the XBPM drawing) are unconfirmed. No double multilayer monochromator appears in the as-built lists, although the FDR and PDR reserved one.

CRL-1 moved from the first optics enclosure (FDR 32.4 m) to the mini-hutch (~43 m), and the lens sets changed (as built 9 and 10 cassettes, all 2D, R ≥ 100 µm, vs 12 stacks in the FDR including 1D lenses and R = 50 µm). Yet the Beamline Directory still quotes the FDR focal sizes (29 × 16 µm, 3.5 × 1.7 µm), so the as-built spot sizes and fluxes need confirmation.

Directory fluxes (e.g. 3.4 × 10¹³ ph/s with CRL-1, 9.4 × 10¹² with CRL-2 and 1.2 × 10¹³ with the KB at 8.8 keV; 3.2 × 10¹¹ and 3.7 × 10¹¹ at 25 keV; and '3 µm × 12 µm' for CRL-2 at high energy) differ from FDR Table 4.58 by roughly a bandwidth factor or 10×; treat them as indicative.

KB working distance: the FDR geometry (vertical mirror 1.0 m and horizontal mirror 0.8 m upstream of the sample), MEDSI 2020 (550 mm) and the SPIE 2025 abstract ('about 650 mm', verified) differ; ~650 mm is the most recent. The full SPIE paper, with measured stability, was not accessible; its abstract states a 55 nrad sample-stability requirement vs 50 nrad in 2020.

Grand Tube dimensions differ by source: 20 m × 2.75 m (Struct. Dyn. 2025), 20.5 m × 2.75 m (shielding paper), '66-foot, ~nine feet' (feature page), '70-foot' (APS news) and '20 m × 3 m' (2023 update). The overall vessel including its heads is probably ~21 m; the inner bore is assumed to be 2.75 m.

Detector specifics are not published: the EIGER 16M variant (EIGER2 X or XE; 400/550 fps suggests XE), the MM-PAD version, and their mounting and travel ranges inside the tube. The beam-stop arrangement for GISAXS and CSSI is undocumented.
The FDR's liquid-surface diffractometer (57 m, with a double-crystal beam tilter for liquid/liquid interfaces) is absent from the as-built lists; whether it was deferred or cancelled is unknown.
Second undulator: the upstream slot is empty, and there is no public schedule for installing the planned planar U21 (the FDR flux tables assume both devices, 4.6 m).

Exact first-light date: the manual says only 'first light in 2024-2'. Whether CSSI (as opposed to GIXS and GI-XPCS) is routinely offered to general users, or mainly in partner or collaborative mode, in run 2026-3 is not stated beyond the 80% general-user allocation 'for GI-SAXS/WAXS/XPCS and CSSI'.
No published 9-ID (post-upgrade) CSSI reconstruction or GI-XPCS paper was found as of 8 October 2026; the science cases cite pre-upgrade 8-ID and P10 work and the legacy 8-ID-E instrument.

The manual's 'first light in 2024-2' predates the 9-ID-A shielding verification (18 December 2024), so it cannot mean X-rays in the hutches. The date the first X-rays reached 9-ID-A or 9-ID-D is not published; technical commissioning began the week of 3 February 2025.
The tag 9ID-BD-3 is used both for the mono flag inside the HDCM (9-ID-A) and for XBPM-1 in 9-ID-MH; the correct assignment is unconfirmed.
The vertical deflection sense of the KB vertical mirror (beam up or down) and the as-built KB angles and coating are not published.
